content.p: At about 11:16 on the morning of Wednesday 29 April 2026, a man with a knife attacked two Jewish men in the street in Golders Green, north-west London, an area with a large Jewish population. One of them, 34-year-old Shloime Rand, was stabbed in the chest as he left a synagogue, prosecutors told a court. The other, 76-year-old Norman Shine, was stabbed in the neck at a bus stop. Shomrim, a volunteer community patrol, said its members detained the attacker, and police Tasered and arrested him. Both victims survived.

Police declared the stabbings a terrorist incident within hours, and the country's terror threat level was raised the next day. Five months later the picture had changed. On 25 September 2026 the accused, 45-year-old Essa Suleiman, pleaded not guilty at the Old Bailey to every charge, and prosecutors said they would no longer allege a terrorist connection. Nothing has been tried or proved. A trial is expected to begin in March 2027.

According to what prosecutors told Westminster Magistrates' Court on 1 May, the day began in Southwark, south London, where Suleiman is alleged to have arrived at the home of a man he had known for years, Ishmail Hussein, and tried to stab him. Prosecutor Emma Harraway said Hussein was a friend of 20 years. The Independent reported her as saying the encounter was at around 7:50 a.m.; police said they were called to a Great Dover Street address at about 8:50 a.m. Hussein suffered minor injuries and called the police. Officers searched the area and an address linked to the suspect, but did not find him.

Prosecutors say he then travelled by public transport to Brent Cross and reached Golders Green shortly after 11 a.m. At 11:16 police were told of people stabbed on Highfield Avenue. Rand, the court heard, had just left a synagogue when he was attacked; he ran back toward it and realised he was bleeding from the chest. He had a punctured lung. Shine was waiting at a bus stop on Golders Green Road. "As Mr. Shine adjusted his kippah, Suleiman ran towards him and set upon him, launching a series of aggressive blows," Harraway told the court, as reported by the Associated Press. Prosecutors said that their clothing made both men clearly recognisable as Orthodox Jews.

CCTV footage obtained by CNN showed one man beside a bus stop putting on his kippah when he was shoved against a sign and repeatedly stabbed, and another walking along a street who was stabbed, shouted at his attacker and managed to run away. Prosecutors said a member of the public who saw the attack on Shine tried to disarm the suspect; further charges relating to the suspect's actions towards that man were under consideration, the Guardian reported.

Shomrim, a volunteer patrol set up in 2009, said a man was seen running along Golders Green Road with a knife, attempting to stab Jewish members of the public. A volunteer was on the scene within about a minute of the call, the Guardian reported. Yonathan Elkouby, 33, a sales worker and father of five, said he heard on his radio that a man had a knife and drove to the scene. He used his car to block the man, then helped police detain him, and said the attacker seemed to be trying to "hit anyone he could". CNN quoted Rabbi Herschel Gluck, who oversees a nearby branch of Shomrim, as saying the volunteers apprehended the attacker and held him until police arrived.

Police said the suspect also tried to stab officers. Body-worn camera footage released by the Metropolitan Police and described by LBC shows an officer shouting at a knife-wielding man to get on the ground; when he stayed on his feet, a second officer was told to use a Taser. The man dropped to his knees but kept hold of a small blade, and the officers struck him on the ground while trying to make him release it. No officers were hurt. Suleiman had what prosecutors called a "medical episode" after being Tasered, was treated in hospital and discharged some hours later.

Shomrim said the two wounded men were treated by Hatzola, the Jewish volunteer ambulance service; police said the London Ambulance Service attended. When charges were announced, police said Rand had left hospital and Shine remained there in a stable condition. Rand told the BBC it was a "miracle" he survived and said: "I feel like God's given me back my life."

Police described the man in custody as a British national born in Somalia. Reports said he came to the United Kingdom lawfully as a child in the early 1990s. Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he had "a history of serious violence and mental health issues". The South London and Maudsley NHS Trust confirmed he had been under the care of its mental health services that week, and the Independent reported that the court was told he was staying at supported accommodation for people leaving a secure hospital. The BBC said the exact address could not be reported for legal reasons.

Police said he had been referred in 2020 to Prevent, the government programme meant to steer people away from extremism, and that the file was closed later that year. They did not say why he was referred. The Middle East Eye, in an opinion piece, also said Suleiman stabbed two police officers and a police dog in 2008. That claim comes from an opinion column.
content.h2: Charges and the case in court
content.p: Counter Terrorism Policing announced that Suleiman, of Camberwell, had been charged with two counts of attempted murder and one of possessing a bladed article in a public place over the Golders Green attack, and with attempted murder over the Great Dover Street incident. He appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 1 May, spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth, did not enter a plea and was sent to the Old Bailey, with a hearing on 15 May.

The charges drew a dispute about emphasis. The Metropolitan Police's post on X said a man would appear in court following an investigation into "two men stabbed in #GoldersGreen", without mentioning the third count, though its full press release did. Journalists including Mehdi Hasan and Owen Jones questioned the omission, according to The National. Barry Malone wrote in Middle East Eye that headlines from outlets including Reuters, the Associated Press and the BBC mentioned only two victims and that Hussein, a Muslim man, received little attention. Those are critics' views, not findings of any court.

On 25 September 2026 at the Old Bailey Suleiman pleaded not guilty to two counts of attempted murder over Golders Green, to a third count of attempted murder relating to the incident at the home of a former acquaintance earlier that day, and to the knife charge, Reuters reported. Prosecutor Deanna Heer said that, after a review, the Crown Prosecution Service had concluded there was no sufficient evidence that the stabbings had a terrorist connection. He was remanded in custody, with his next appearance listed for 15 January and the trial for March 2027.

In a message to London communities on 28 September, the Metropolitan Police said the CPS still believed the evidence showed the defendant's actions to be hate crimes, which it will put to the court as an aggravating factor when sentencing. It acknowledged the news might cause concern in the Jewish community. The message said the seriousness with which the matter was being treated had not changed. Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said she recognised the impact on the three victims and on the Jewish community.

An hour or so after the attack, a post in the name of Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, known as HAYI, appeared on Telegram, according to the Guardian. Counter-terrorism police were aware of it. The group had first appeared online on 9 March and had claimed attacks on Jewish sites in Belgium and the Netherlands, as well as several arson attacks in north London. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said authorities were examining whether the claim was credible or "opportunistic". The Guardian reported that investigators saw no initial evidence of Iranian state direction of the Golders Green attack and thought HAYI's statements most likely opportunistic, although their lead hypothesis for the group itself was a degree of Iranian state direction. NPR noted that security experts warned the name might be a flag of convenience rather than a coherent group.

The stabbing came after a run of attacks on Jewish and Iran-related targets in the same part of London. Four Hatzola ambulances were set alight in Golders Green in the early hours of 23 March. On 28 August 2026 four men pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to arson being reckless whether life would be endangered, and a fifth pleaded not guilty to assisting an offender, the Metropolitan Police said. The Guardian put the damage at about £1m. Counter Terrorism Policing said 28 people had been arrested across the linked investigations since the ambulance attack. In mid-April, the Metropolitan Police said none of the earlier incidents had been declared terrorism, and that officers were keeping an open mind about motive. None of that has been shown to connect to Suleiman.

Prime Minister Keir Starmer called it an "antisemitic attack" and "utterly appalling", and thanked Shomrim, Hatzola and the police. Buckingham Palace said King Charles III was "naturally deeply concerned, in particular about the impact for the Jewish community". Finchley and Golders Green MP Sarah Sackman said the prime minister would convene a COBRA meeting. On 30 April the terror threat level moved from substantial to severe, which the government said reflected a rising threat from Islamist and extreme right-wing individuals and small groups as well as this attack. Ministers called antisemitism an emergency and announced 25 million pounds for police patrols and protection around synagogues, schools and community centres.

Starmer was heckled by about 100 protesters during a visit to Golders Green, NPR reported. Rowley said the Metropolitan Police needed an extra 300 officers to provide permanent protection for Jewish communities. Shomrim volunteers said they had no government funding and were stretched; Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged support for them.

A second row concerned the arrest itself. Green Party leader Zack Polanski shared a post claiming officers had been "repeatedly and violently kicking a mentally ill man in the head". Rowley wrote to him calling that "inaccurate and misinformed commentary", and said officers had feared the man might have an explosive device. Critics of Rowley condemned his letter as a political intervention, The National reported. Polanski apologised for sharing a tweet "in haste".
